107 Wessex House St. Davids, Pa. 19087
POR
August 22, 1972
The Hon. Rogers C. B. Norton Secretary of the Interior Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Secretary Forton:
There seems to me to be justification for nation-wide disappointment in the Department's environmental statement published in the <u>Federal Register</u> for June 2, 1972, pertaining to the use of off-road vehicles on public lands.
That such a document should have been prepared by the new Bureau of Cutdoor Recreation seems unfortunate; and being prepared by that bureau, is understandable why the only people likely to find satisfaction in it are the manufacturers and users of off-road vehicles. (Soon after BCR was established and its activities became clear, I recommended its abolishment or giving it the sole duty of caring for the national recreation areas. By foremost reason for suggesting abolishment was because it usurped and still usurps certain prerogatives of the National Park Service, in spite of the Service's having been in business since 1916 and knowing its objectives and functions better than could any other organization.)
The statement seems to me to fall short of reflecting the spirit of the executive order issued by the White House on February 8, 1972.
In an article entitled "Snowmobiles in the National Parks", published in American Forests in April, (copy sent to you,) I said, "Snowmobile operators and the operators of other off-road vehicles have the same right as anyone to seek the spiritual uplift that the national parks and their wildlife and plant life alone can give; but they have no special privilege to go into the sanctuaries with their din and destructive effects to land, vegetation and wildlife, and their annoyance to other visitors." This viewpoint imposes no hardship or unfairness. That is right and fair for one is right and fair for all.
Although the article is specific about national parks and national nature monuments, why should the same thinking not serve as a basis also for public use of national wildlife refuges and BIM lands? Will we not be playing dangerously with vast acreages of our federal lands and cause endless annoyance to other visitors by taking any less stringent viewpoint? As now written, the statement might well have been the work of off-road vehicle manufacturers and users. It simply does not face facts.
ly hope is that the Department of the Interior will regard the draft in the <u>Tederal Toristor</u> as a preliminary one and that a new version will be written that will tackle this ratter from the point of view that all of us have the right to go into these lands, but that none of us has a special privilege to do so in ways that will result in harm to the environment, destroying the very things we go there to enjoy.
Sincerely,

Deveroux Subcher
